```{r}
library(terra)

library(sf)

ppt_days <- rast("ne_ppt_2012aug.tif")

n_cells <- ncell(ppt_days)
n_na1 <- global(ppt_days[[1]], "isNA")[1, 1]
mean_true <- round(global(ppt_days[[1]], "mean", na.rm = TRUE)[1, 1], 2)

n_9999 <- sum(values(raw) == -9999)
```

# How this lecture works

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## What you will and will not learn today

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The plan

Weather, elevation, soil and satellite images come as **raster data**: a grid of cells, each with a value. An AI assistant can read any raster format and compute anything on it. What it cannot do is:

+ know what the numbers in the cells mean: their units, their scale, which value means "no data"
+ know where the grid should be
+ tell whether a value it computed is believable

Those are your job. So today is about:

1. **The concept**: what a raster is, and what has to be true before its values can be used
2. **Reading code**: recognising what a line of raster code does
3. **Asking AI**: what to put in your request
4. **Checking**: what to print for every raster, and why

### Directions

+ Ask your AI assistant to install the `terra` and `tidyterra` packages if you have not already. `terra` reads and computes on rasters; `tidyterra` lets `ggplot2` draw them.
+ The data files used on these slides sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path here is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with `here::here()` (lecture 03-1).

:::

# The concept

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## A raster is a grid of cells

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The idea

A raster covers a rectangle with a grid of equal cells. Each cell holds one value. What describes the grid:

| Term | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Extent** | The rectangle the grid covers: lowest and highest x, lowest and highest y |
| **Resolution** | The width and height of one cell, in the units of the CRS |
| **Rows and columns** | How many cells down and across |
| **CRS** | What the x and y numbers mean, as in lecture 09-1 |
| **Layers** | A raster can hold several grids on the same cells, for example one per day. Each layer has a name. |

A cell with no value (outside the area measured, or a failed reading) holds `NA`, R's missing value, if the file says which value means "no data".

### A whole raster

Daily precipitation in millimetres on 1 August 2012, from PRISM (a US weather dataset), for the rectangle around Nebraska. Cells outside Nebraska hold no data.

```{r}
#| label: whole
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster(data = ppt_days[[1]]) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Precipitation\n(mm)", na.value = "transparent") +
  theme_void()
```

### Close up

The 8-by-8 block of cells in the north-west corner of the state, with the value of each cell written in it:

```{r}
#| label: close-up
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.5
block <- crop(ppt_days[[1]], ext(-104.06, -103.73, 42.68, 43.02))
cells <- as.data.frame(block, xy = TRUE, na.rm = FALSE)
names(cells)[3] <- "value"
ggplot(cells, aes(x, y, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(is.na(value), "NA", round(value, 1))), size = 4) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Precipitation\n(mm)", na.value = "grey85", begin = 0.4) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_void()
```

Each square is one cell, about 4 km across, and the number in it is the whole of what the raster knows about that square.

:::

## What a raster file does and does not say

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Stored, and not always stored

| Always in the file | Sometimes in the file, sometimes only in the documentation |
|---|---|
| The numbers in the cells | Which value means "no data" (often -9999) |
| The extent, resolution, rows, columns | The **units** (millimetres or inches, degrees C or F) |
| The number of layers | The **scale**: values stored as whole numbers, such as hundredths of a millimetre, to save space |
| Usually the CRS | What each layer is (which date), beyond a name |

Whatever is not in the file, only you can tell the AI, from the documentation of the data.

### Vector or raster

| | Vector (lecture 09-1) | Raster |
|---|---|---|
| Stores | separate features, each with a shape | one value per cell of a grid |
| One row or cell is | a county, a well | a 4 km square |
| Typical data | boundaries, locations, roads | weather, elevation, satellite images |
| R package | `sf` | `terra` |

Both need a CRS, and both must share a CRS with any layer they are combined with.

:::

# How raster code is written

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## Reading a raster

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The pattern

```{r}
#| eval: false
raster <- rast("path/to/file")
```

| Part | What it is | Required? |
|---|---|---|
| `raster <-` | The name the raster will have inside R | Needed to keep the result |
| `rast` | The reader from `terra`, for every raster format | Yes |
| `"path/to/file"` | Where the file is. `c("file1", "file2")` reads several files as layers of one raster. | **Yes, the only required input** |

A real line, and what R prints for it:

```{r}
#| label: read-ppt-days
ppt_days <- rast("ne_ppt_2012aug.tif")
ppt_days
```

### Reading the printout

| Line | What it says here |
|---|---|
| `size` | `r nrow(ppt_days)` rows, `r ncol(ppt_days)` columns, `r nlyr(ppt_days)` layers |
| `resolution` | one cell is `r round(res(ppt_days)[1], 4)` by `r round(res(ppt_days)[2], 4)`, in degrees because of the CRS |
| `extent` | longitude `r round(xmin(ppt_days), 1)` to `r round(xmax(ppt_days), 1)`, latitude `r round(ymin(ppt_days), 1)` to `r round(ymax(ppt_days), 1)`: Nebraska |
| `coord. ref.` | the CRS: longitude and latitude, NAD83 (EPSG 4269) |
| `names` | one name per layer: here, the date |
| `min values`, `max values` | the smallest and largest value in each layer, ignoring no-data cells |

Most of the checks for a raster are on this printout.

### Formats

The same reader opens all of them:

| Extension | Format | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| `.tif` | GeoTIFF, the most common | satellite images, elevation, most downloads |
| `.bil` (with `.hdr`) | Band interleaved by line | PRISM weather data |
| `.nc` | netCDF, often many layers | climate data such as gridMET, often one layer per day |
| `.asc` | ASCII grid, plain text | older data |

### Writing

```{r}
#| eval: false
writeRaster(raster, "path/to/file.tif")
```

The extension picks the format. `overwrite = TRUE` is needed to replace an existing file. A raster cannot go into a csv without losing the grid.

:::

## Doing things with a raster

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The pattern

Most raster functions take the raster first and return a new raster:

```{r}
#| eval: false
result <- raster_function(raster, other_inputs)
```

| Function | What it does | Default that matters |
|---|---|---|
| `raster1 + raster2`, `raster * 10`, `log(raster)` | Arithmetic, cell by cell. Rasters must share extent and resolution. | |
| `raster[[2]]` or `raster[["name"]]` | One layer | |
| `global(raster, "mean")` | One number per layer, over all cells | Without `na.rm = TRUE`, a single `NA` makes the result `NA` |
| `classify(raster, cbind(-9999, NA))` | Replaces values, here -9999 by `NA` | |
| `aggregate(raster, fact = 5)` | Coarser cells: each 5-by-5 block becomes one cell | Averages the block (`fun = "mean"`) |
| `resample(raster, template)` | Moves values onto another grid | Interpolates between cells (`method = "bilinear"`) |
| `project(raster, "EPSG:5070")` | Moves the raster into another CRS | Recomputes every cell value |
| `crop()`, `mask()`, `extract()` | Combine a raster with vector data | Lecture 09-6 |

### One real example

The total over the five days, cell by cell, and its largest value:

```{r}
#| label: total
ppt_total <- sum(ppt_days)
global(ppt_total, "max", na.rm = TRUE)
```

`sum()` over the layers of one raster adds them cell by cell, giving a raster with one layer.

### Variations you will see

+ `terra::rast(...)`: the package name in front
+ `rast(here::here("data", "ppt.tif"))`: the path built by another function
+ `ppt_days$ppt_2012_08_01`: one layer by name, like a column of a table
+ `ggplot() + geom_spatraster(data = raster)`: a map of a raster, from `tidyterra` (lecture 09-3)

:::

# What has to be true

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## Conditions for raster values to be right

::: {.panel-tabset}

### The conditions

1. **The no-data value is declared**, so cells without data are `NA`, not a number such as -9999.
2. **The units and scale are known**, so a stored 7381 is read as 73.81 millimetres.
3. **The grid is where the place is**: the CRS and extent are right.
4. **Each layer is what you think**: the right date, the right variable.
5. **Every operation's default fits the kind of value**: averaging works for amounts such as rainfall, not for codes such as 1 = corn, 2 = soybean.
6. **A raster combined with vector data shares its CRS.** Transform the vector layer to the raster's CRS, not the other way: projecting a raster recomputes its values.

### With and without an error

Raster operations stop with an error when two rasters do not share extent and resolution, or a file does not exist. Conditions 1 to 5 failing gives numbers with **no error**: the silent failures on the next slide are three of them.

:::

## Silent failures: cell values misread

::: {.panel-tabset}

### An undeclared no-data value

`ne_ppt_raw.tif` holds the same 1 August 2012 precipitation, stored the way some data providers store it: -9999 in the cells outside Nebraska, and no line in the file saying that -9999 means "no data".

```{r}
#| label: raw
raw <- rast("ne_ppt_raw.tif")
raw
```

The average over the cells:

```{r}
#| label: raw-mean
global(raw, "mean")
```

An average daily precipitation of `r mean_raw` millimetres, impossible, and no error. `r format(n_9999, big.mark = ",")` cells hold -9999 and were averaged with the rest. The printout above shows it: `min value: -9999`.

### Values in a scale

The largest value in the same file is 7381. 7,381 millimetres in a day is impossible: the file stores **hundredths** of a millimetre as whole numbers. Only the documentation says so. Both fixes together, declare -9999 as no data, then divide by 100:

```{r}
#| label: raw-fixed
fixed <- classify(raw, cbind(-9999, NA)) / 100
global(fixed, c("min", "max", "mean"), na.rm = TRUE)
```

Now the values run from 0 to 73.8 millimetres, and the average is `r mean_true` millimetres, the same as the file that declares its no-data value and units.

### Averaging codes

A small land-cover raster where 1 means corn and 2 means soybean, made coarser by `aggregate()`, which averages by default:

```{r}
#| label: categories
landcover <- rast(nrows = 4, ncols = 4, xmin = 0, xmax = 4, ymin = 0, ymax = 4,
                  vals = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1))
values(aggregate(landcover, fact = 2))
```

Values of 1.25 and 1.5 are neither corn nor soybean, and nothing warns you. For codes, the right rule is the most common value in each block, `fun = "modal"`:

```{r}
#| label: categories-modal
values(aggregate(landcover, fact = 2, fun = "modal"))
```

`resample()` has the same problem when codes are stored as plain numbers: its default, `"bilinear"`, interpolates between neighbouring cells. Tell it `method = "near"`. (If the raster is declared categorical, `terra` uses `"near"` itself; `aggregate()` averages either way.) `project()`, which moves a raster to another CRS, has the same default and needs the same instruction.

:::

# Asking AI

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## Working with AI on your own research

The way of working from lecture 02-1, "Working with AI on your own research", applies unchanged:

1. **You ask.** Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
2. **The AI writes into a Quarto document** (`.qmd`). Code goes into code chunks, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
3. **You render** the `.qmd` to HTML.
4. **You read the HTML** and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.

A raster's printout, its value ranges and a quick map are checks you judge by eye. In the HTML they sit next to the code that produced them, and the document records which no-data value and scale you told the AI to use, and why.

:::{.callout-note}
Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines, the **closing instructions**; the full text is under **Recommended requests** near the end.
:::

## Look before you ask

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Read the documentation

Raster data almost always comes with documentation: a README, a metadata page, a `.txt` or `.xml` file next to the data. Find in it:

1. **The variable and its units**: precipitation in millimetres, temperature in degrees C
2. **The scale**: are values stored as they are, or multiplied (by 10, 100, 10,000) to make whole numbers?
3. **The no-data value**: often -9999, sometimes 0 or 255
4. **The CRS**
5. **What each layer is**: which date, which band of a satellite image

### Print the raster before computing anything

The printout of `rast()` reads only the file's description and, if the file stores them, its smallest and largest values, so it is quick even for a large file. If the printout has no `min value` line, ask for the range before anything else.

```{r}
#| label: look-raw
rast("ne_ppt_raw.tif")
```

From this alone: one layer, longitude and latitude around Nebraska, values from -9999 to 7381. Compare that with the documentation **before** asking for any calculation.

:::

## What to put in your request

The AI knows every `terra` function. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

1. **The file**: name, format, where it is in your project
2. **What the values mean**: the variable, its units, its scale
3. **The no-data value**
4. **The CRS**, and **what each layer is**
5. **What you want back**: which layers, which units, which calculation, and for codes, that values must not be averaged
6. **Ask for checks**: next section
7. **The closing instructions**

:::{.callout-tip title="Using an agent in your editor or terminal?"}
An agent such as Claude Code can open the raster and print it for itself. It still cannot know a scale or a no-data value that is only in the documentation. Write those down **before** it runs.
:::

## A weak request and a strong one

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Weak

```text
Load the precipitation raster and give me the average rainfall.
```

A typical reply:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ppt <- rast("ppt.tif")
global(ppt, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
```

On a file like `ne_ppt_raw.tif` this prints `r mean_raw`, with no error: the -9999 cells and the hundredths are both taken at face value.

### Strong

An example for a precipitation file like the one on the "Silent failures" slide:

```text
In my R project, data/ppt_raw.tif is a GeoTIFF of daily precipitation
on 1 August 2012 around Nebraska, one layer. Its documentation says:
values are hundredths of a millimetre stored as whole numbers, -9999
means no data, and the CRS is NAD83 longitude and latitude (EPSG 4269).

Read it, mark -9999 as missing, and convert the values to millimetres,
in a raster called ppt. Then print the average precipitation over the
cells with data.

Check: the CRS (I expect EPSG 4269), the extent (I expect longitude
between -104 and -95 and latitude between 40 and 43), the smallest and
largest value after conversion (I expect 0 and something below 150 mm),
and the number of missing cells. Draw a quick map of the raster.

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/weather.qmd, under the
heading "Read the precipitation", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.
```

### What came back

In the rendered HTML, a sentence, then the chunk it describes.

Read the raster, mark -9999 as missing, and convert hundredths of a millimetre to millimetres.

```{r}
#| label: ai-read
#| eval: false
ppt <- rast(here::here("data", "ppt_raw.tif"))
ppt <- classify(ppt, cbind(-9999, NA)) / 100
```

Print the checks against what was expected, then the average.

```{r}
#| label: ai-check
#| eval: false
rng <- global(ppt, c("min", "max"), na.rm = TRUE)
cat("CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG", crs(ppt, describe = TRUE)$code, "\n")
cat("longitude: expected -104 to -95, got", round(xmin(ppt), 1), "to", round(xmax(ppt), 1), "\n")
cat("latitude: expected 40 to 43, got", round(ymin(ppt), 1), "to", round(ymax(ppt), 1), "\n")
cat("smallest value: expected 0, got", rng$min, "\n")
cat("largest value: expected below 150, got", rng$max, "\n")
cat("missing cells: expected some (the rectangle reaches outside Nebraska), got", global(ppt, "isNA")[1, 1], "of", ncell(ppt), "\n")
global(ppt, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
```

`crs(ppt, describe = TRUE)$code` pulls the EPSG code out of the CRS description. The output is in the next section.

:::

# Checking the result

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## What to check for every raster

::: {.panel-tabset}

### What to ask for, and why

The AI can write the checking code. It cannot know the right answers. Ask for these after reading a raster and after each step that changes its values:

| | Ask the AI to print | Catches | What only you can supply |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | the CRS | a missing or wrong CRS | the CRS from the documentation |
| 2 | rows, columns, resolution, number of layers | the wrong file, a layer missing | what the documentation says |
| 3 | the extent | a grid in the wrong place, or in metres when you expected degrees | where the place is |
| 4 | the name of each layer | layers in the wrong order, the wrong dates | which date or variable each layer is |
| 5 | the smallest and largest value of each layer | an undeclared no-data value, a scale not applied, the wrong units | a believable range, in known units |
| 6 | the number of missing (`NA`) cells | no-data cells counted as values (zero missing where some should be) | roughly how many cells lie outside the area |
| 7 | a quick map of each layer | anything the numbers did not show | what the pattern should look like |

### Asking for them

One sentence at the end of your request:

```text
Print the CRS, the extent, the resolution, the name, smallest and
largest value of each layer, and the number of missing cells, and draw
a quick map of each layer.
```

Better, with what you expect:

```text
I expect EPSG <code>, longitude between <west> and <east> and latitude
between <south> and <north>, layers named <names>, and values between
<lowest> and <highest> <units>. Print each check on its own line as
"name of check: expected X, got Y".
```

### Reading the HTML

What the checking code on the previous slide printed, run on `ne_ppt_raw.tif`:

```{r}
#| label: chk-run
#| echo: false
ppt_chk <- classify(rast("ne_ppt_raw.tif"), cbind(-9999, NA)) / 100
rng <- global(ppt_chk, c("min", "max"), na.rm = TRUE)
cat("CRS: expected EPSG 4269, got EPSG", crs(ppt_chk, describe = TRUE)$code, "\n")
cat("longitude: expected -104 to -95, got", round(xmin(ppt_chk), 1), "to", round(xmax(ppt_chk), 1), "\n")
cat("latitude: expected 40 to 43, got", round(ymin(ppt_chk), 1), "to", round(ymax(ppt_chk), 1), "\n")
cat("smallest value: expected 0, got", rng$min, "\n")
cat("largest value: expected below 150, got", rng$max, "\n")
cat("missing cells: expected some (the rectangle reaches outside Nebraska), got", global(ppt_chk, "isNA")[1, 1], "of", ncell(ppt_chk), "\n")
global(ppt_chk, "mean", na.rm = TRUE)
```

Every check passes. `r format(n_na1, big.mark = ",")` of `r format(n_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells are missing, about `r round(100 * n_na1 / n_cells)`%: the rectangle around Nebraska includes parts of other states, and the cells there have no data. Had the -9999 not been declared, this line would say 0, and the smallest value -99.99.

:::

## Checks that come from knowing the data

The checks above apply to any raster. Checks from what you know about **this** variable are stronger:

+ Precipitation is never negative, and a daily total above a few hundred millimetres would be a record.
+ Five different days should not have identical values. A file in which two layers are the same is a file with a mistake in it.

```text
Using the raster ppt_days with five daily layers, print the smallest value
of each layer (I expect 0 or more), and for each pair of consecutive
days, whether the two layers are identical (I expect not).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/weather.qmd, under the
heading "Check against the data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk,
write one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build
every path with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the
document to HTML.
```

The AI's code, and what it printed:

```{r}
#| label: chk-data
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code the AI wrote"
mins <- global(ppt_days, "min", na.rm = TRUE)$min
cat("smallest value per day: expected 0 or more, got", round(mins, 2), "\n")
for (i in 1:(nlyr(ppt_days) - 1)) {
  same <- all(values(ppt_days[[i]]) == values(ppt_days[[i + 1]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  cat(names(ppt_days)[i], "and", names(ppt_days)[i + 1], "identical: expected FALSE, got", same, "\n")
}
```

All pass. When a check like this fails, the code is usually not the problem: the file is. Stop, and ask whoever produced it.

## Your turn: read the AI's code

```{r}
#| label: lc-resample
#| include: false
template <- rast(nrows = 3, ncols = 3, xmin = 0.3, xmax = 3.3, ymin = 0.3, ymax = 3.3)
lc_moved <- values(resample(landcover, template))[, 1]
lc_example <- sort(unique(round(lc_moved, 2)))
lc_example <- lc_example[lc_example %% 1 != 0][1:3]
```

A student has a land-cover raster, where 1 means corn, 2 soybean and 3 pasture, stored as plain numbers, and a weather raster on a different grid. They asked an AI to "put the land cover on the weather grid", and got this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
landcover <- rast(here::here("data", "landcover.tif"))
weather <- rast(here::here("data", "weather.tif"))
landcover_on_weather <- resample(landcover, weather)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Questions

A. What does each line do?

B. Which line gives a wrong result **without** an error, and what will the result contain?

C. Which check would catch it?

D. What should the request have said?

### Answers

A. Reads the land-cover raster; reads the weather raster; moves the land-cover values onto the weather grid.

B. Line 3. Without a `method`, `resample()` interpolates between neighbouring cells (`"bilinear"`). Codes are not amounts, so the result holds values between the codes. On the 4-by-4 land-cover raster from the "Silent failures" slide, moved to a shifted 3-by-3 grid, it gives values such as `r paste(lc_example, collapse = ", ")`: neither corn nor soybean.

C. The list of distinct values before and after. Before: 1, 2 and 3. After: many values that are not whole numbers. The smallest and largest value would not catch it, because every interpolated value lies between them.

D. That the values are codes that must not be averaged or interpolated, so that each new cell takes the value of the nearest old cell (`method = "near"`), and to print the distinct values before and after.

:::

# Recommended requests

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## Requests you can copy

Copy one, then replace every `<...>` with what **you** found in the data's documentation and printout. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Closing instructions

The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave "expected X, got Y" as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:

```text
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
```

A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your `.qmd` and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.

### Look at a raster


# Summary

<html><div style='float:left'></div><hr color='#EB811B' size=1px width=796px></html>

## What you must understand, and what the AI can write

| You need to understand | The AI can write |
|---|---|
| What a raster is: extent, resolution, CRS, layers | `rast()` and the reading of any format |
| What the cell values mean: units, scale, no-data value, from the documentation | `classify()`, the conversion |
| What each layer is | Naming and selecting layers |
| Whether a value is an amount or a code, and so how it may be combined | `aggregate()`, `resample()` with the right rule |
| What believable values are for your variable and place | The checking code |

**Every raster:** read its documentation and write down units, scale, no-data value, CRS and a believable range. Print the raster before computing anything. Ask the AI to write the code and the checks into your `.qmd`. Render it, and judge the HTML against what you wrote down.
